3.3 Food access, cars and diabetes

Food-desert tracts had about 1.5 percentage points higher diabetes prevalence than other tracts (95% CI 1.0-2.0), after accounting for urban or rural status and state. Each 1-point higher share of households without a vehicle was associated with a 0.13-point higher prevalence (95% CI 0.11-0.14); in other words, a 10-point difference in households without a car was associated with about 1.3 more points of diabetes. Urban tracts had about 1.0 point lower prevalence than rural tracts, and Michigan tracts about 0.7 points higher than California tracts. Adding the share of residents aged 65 and older changed little (food desert 1.4 points, 95% CI 0.9-1.9). I found no clear difference between the states in the association with food deserts (p = 0.12). Together, these measures explained 12.5% of the variation in diabetes prevalence between tracts.

The part of diabetes prevalence that the model did not explain was similar in neighboring tracts (Moran's I of the residuals 0.64, p = 0.001), so I also fitted a spatial lag model. In this model, the associations became smaller but remained: food desert, 1.2 points (95% CI 0.7-1.7); households without a vehicle, 0.10 points per 1-point increase (95% CI 0.09-0.12).

3.4 Food deserts hidden by smaller stores

When only large grocery stores were counted (LRAM 2019), 648 California tracts and 352 Michigan tracts were food deserts. When all SNAP-authorized stores were counted (SRAM, 2025), this fell to 154 and 52. Most of the difference was in tracts that were food deserts by the large-store measure but not by the all-store measure: 567 in California and 329 in Michigan. Fewer tracts went the other way, being food deserts only when all SNAP-authorized stores were counted: 73 in California and 29 in Michigan, possibly reflecting store changes between 2019 and 2025.

The gap was largest in Metro Detroit. All 97 Metro Detroit tracts that were food deserts by the large-store measure appeared to have access when smaller SNAP-authorized stores were counted. Among high-diabetes tracts, 51 of 358 in Metro Detroit (14%) were hidden in this way, home to about 19,500 adults with diabetes, compared with 30 of 1,000 high-diabetes tracts in Metro Los Angeles (3%), home to about 15,600 adults with diabetes (Figure 2). 4).

The problem was not whether the food was healthy. It was whether the person could buy it near home. In hidden tracts, the chatbots recommended 16 foods on average, and about 5 of them (30%) are not reliably sold by the kinds of stores these tracts have nearby: convenience, small grocery, and dollar stores. The buyable-nearby score (Score B) was 0.70 (range 0.55-0.86): 0.67 for ChatGPT, 0.68 for Claude and 0.76 for Gemini, and 0.72 in Metro Detroit and 0.69 in Metro Los Angeles (Figure 3). The foods most often out of reach were fresh chicken, cabbage, yogurt, carrots, and fresh leafy greens. The chatbots changed their advice only a little by place. Fresh perishable foods made up 30% of recommended foods in hidden tracts and 33% in comparison tracts (p = 0.047). Only 4 of 60 answers, and only 1 of the 30 for hidden tracts, mentioned dollar, corner, or neighborhood stores, the kinds of stores people in hidden tracts rely on. ChatGPT and Gemini also named specific local places: 41 street addresses in 16 ChatGPT answers and 14 in 11 Gemini answers. Claude named none. I located 51 of the 55 addresses. Their median distance from the person's tract was 1.3 miles; only 27% were within 1 mile, and 22% were more than 3 miles away (Figure 4). In hidden tracts, only 1 of 7 grocery stores named was within 1 mile. All 20 grocery stores named were active SNAP-authorized stores at the stated address in the USDA retailer list, although one was given under a name last used in 2019. All 20 grocery stores were named by ChatGPT; all 14 places Gemini named were food pantries or community programs.

Overall, 45 of the 55 places (82%) were confirmed at the stated address. Seven (13%) had a clear problem, and all of them were food pantries or community programs: a wrong address (3), a different business at that address (1), or a food program that could not be confirmed (3). Gemini described 10 places as being in or near the person's ZIP code or neighborhood; 4 of these were in a different ZIP code or 2.4 to 6.6 miles away. Score A = share of five diabetes nutrition points present. Score B = share of recommended foods sold by the store types near the tract (hidden: convenience, small grocery and dollar stores only; comparison: a large grocery store is also nearby, so Score B = 1 by design). Foods rated 'maybe' in the food-to-store table counted as not sold. p = Mann-Whitney test (Mann & Whitney, 1947). Five nutrition points from the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2026.

4. Discussion

This study asked a simple question: before AI tells patients what to eat, does it know where they live? I found three things. First, high diabetes and food deserts overlapped in only a small number of tracts (71 in California and 19 in Michigan), and almost none were inside the two metros. Second, the newer USDA map, which counts every SNAPauthorized store, hides food deserts. This was most striking in Metro Detroit, where every tract that was a food desert by the large-store measure looked like it had access once smaller stores were counted; 51 high-diabetes tracts, home to about 19,500 adults with diabetes, were hidden this way. Third, AI chatbots gave healthy diabetes advice, but in these hidden tracts about 3 in 10 recommended foods are not reliably sold by the kinds of stores nearby, and the places they named were mostly beyond walking distance.

The link between food deserts and diabetes was real but modest. Food-desert tracts had about 1.5 points higher prevalence, and all my measures together explained 12.5% of the variation between tracts. This fits earlier work. A meta-analysis found no convincing evidence that the food environment alone explains diabetes (den Braver et al., 2018), and in a national study, food outlets explained little of the neighborhood gradient in diabetes (Thorpe et al., 2022). In New York City, USDA low access ranked low among the neighborhood predictors of diabetes (Tanner et al., 2024). In my data, the share of households without a car was also a clear and consistent signal, and it held up in the spatial model. So I read these results as overlap, not cause: they show where diabetes and poor access meet, not that distance causes diabetes. But even if food outlets explain little of who gets diabetes, local access still limits which diet advice people can actually follow.

The hidden food deserts are the clearest finding of this paper. In Metro Detroit, all 97 tracts that were food deserts by the large-store measure appeared to have access once convenience, small grocery and dollar stores were counted. Detroit researchers have warned about this. A study of Detroit births found no link between the USDA low-access measure and diabetes, and noted that supermarket-based definitions miss the corner and dollar stores common in the city (McClain et al., 2026). Twenty years ago, the poorest Black neighborhoods in Detroit were already about 1.1 miles farther from a chain supermarket than the poorest White neighborhoods (Zenk et al., 2005). Store type matters too. Across 19,607 urban US tracts, access to dollar stores was linked to more diabetes and access to grocery stores to less, and dollar stores made up over 40% of nearby stores in the Midwest and South but under 25% in the Pacific region (Bruellman et al., 2026). The gap I found between Metro Detroit (14% of high-diabetes tracts hidden) and Metro Los Angeles (3%) fits that pattern. Because the all-store map is now USDA's current measure, programs that use it to decide where to send food help could miss these neighborhoods.

The AI pilot shows why this matters for AI tools. The chatbots gave healthy advice, and every answer mentioned budget and getting around without a car. But mentioning place is not the same as using it. In hidden tracts, about 5 of the 16 recommended foods were not reliably sold nearby, and the chatbots shifted only slightly toward shelf-stable foods (30% fresh foods versus 33% in comparison tracts). This is close to what Logan et al. (2025) saw: Gemini showed maps of nearby stores, but location had little effect on the foods it recommended. Dietitians reviewing AI meal plans for type 2 diabetes also noted that the tools did not assess access to food (Bayram et al., 2025). When ChatGPT and Gemini did name local places, most were more than a mile away, and about 1 in 8 had a clear error, all of them food pantries or community programs. Claude named no places at all. That avoids wrong addresses, but it leaves the patient without local help. To my knowledge, this is the first study to check AI diabetes diet advice against the kinds of stores near where patients live.

Who should act on this? I see three groups: the teams that deliver food-is-medicine care, the payers that fund it, and the people who build and govern AI nutrition tools. The ADA review highlights community health workers' roles in assessing social needs and linking patients to services, and calls for Medicaid flexibility to cover social care (Hill-Briggs et al., 2021); mapping double-burden neighborhoods could help target these resources. Screening alone is not enough: food insecurity screening without a warm hand-off to nutrition or food-is-medicine programs is unlikely to improve clinical outcomes (Levi et al., 2023), which places a premium on knowing which neighborhoods lack nearby food sources.

Payers have a financial case to act: if medically tailored meals designed by registered dietitians were covered nationally for adults with diet-sensitive conditions and functional limitations (44.9% of whom had diabetes), an estimated 1.6 million hospitalizations and $13.6 billion in net health care costs could be averted each year, yet these meals are not a covered benefit in Medicare or Medicaid (Hager et al., 2022). State-level modeling estimated 923,568 eligible adults in California, with net savings of about $3,022 per person per year (95% uncertainty interval -$1,309 to $7,622), and five-year net savings of about $14.8 billion in California and $5.7 billion in Michigan, although every uncertainty interval included zero (Deng et al., 2025, online supplement). By January 2025, 16 states had approved or proposed Medicaid Section 1115 waivers for these meals (Deng et al., 2025). Neither model accounts for where patients live or their local food access; tract-level mapping could help payers target these benefits. Policy readiness differs between my two regions: California is among 16 states approved for or pending Medicaid Section 1115 waivers that include food-is-medicine services, whereas Michigan is not (Shah et al., 2026). Health systems are urged to screen for nutrition risk, stratify patients, and refer them in a closed loop to registered dietitian nutritionists, social workers or community health workers (Shah et al., 2026).

Money for food helps, but it does not solve distance. In a Los Angeles produceprescription program for Medicaid patients with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, the share of people who could regularly get healthy food rose from 23.2% to 38.7% in six months. Yet the share who had no car or transportation to reach healthy food barely changed (44.4% before, 43.2% after) (Caldwell et al., 2026). Food benefits may work better when they are paired with home delivery, or aimed at neighborhoods with poor access.

AI chatbots are already embedded in food-is-medicine programs: a bilingual GPT-3.5based chatbot supported a produce-prescription trial for high-risk, predominantly Hispanic pregnant women in Houston, with safeguards limited to prompt design and weekly review of chat logs, and without consideration of users' store access, transportation or cost (Macias-Navarro et al., 2026). Its developers recommended constraining responses to curated clinical sources through retrieval-augmented generation (Macias-Navarro et al., 2026); my findings suggest such tools should also be grounded in local food-access data. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and the American Society for Nutrition now call on practitioners to set standards for how AI is designed, deployed and evaluated, and to audit tools for bias with equity built in from the start (Murofushi et al., 2026); yet their guidance does not address food access, cost or other social determinants when AI gives dietary advice. Food-is-medicine implementation guidance already envisions AI-enabled decision support to match patients to food-is-medicine tiers and AI-driven dietary platforms that deliver real-time personalized nutrition recommendations (Shah et al., 2026), but does not specify how such recommendations should be checked against what is available where patients live. I propose a simple place-aware audit check as one way to operationalize this guidance: before an AI tool recommends foods, test whether those foods are available and affordable in the user's neighborhood.

4.1 Limitations

The AI pilot has its own limits. It used one synthetic person, 20 tracts and one answer per chatbot per tract, collected on two days in October 2026. Chatbot answers change over time and even between identical prompts: in one repeated run, Claude showed a nearby-store card the first time but not the second. The chatbots were also accessed differently: ChatGPT and Gemini logged out, and Claude signed in with memory turned off. Score B relies on a table of what each store type usually sells, not on an audit of real shelves, and comparison tracts scored 1 by design. Score B also ignores price: in a market-basket study in Mississippi, convenience stores charged about 35% more than supermarkets for fruits and vegetables (Canales et al., 2021), so the share of advice that people can actually afford to follow may be lower than Score B suggests. Scoring was done by a rule-based script that I checked on 20% of answers, and the address check relied partly on AI-assisted web searches, which I checked on five places and, for all grocery stores, against the USDA SNAP retailer list.

USDA food-access measures capture only geographic proximity, not affordability, store quality, transit, online purchasing or food assistance (USDA ERS, 2026); SRAM counts all SNAP-authorized retailers, including convenience and dollar stores, while LRAM relies on 2019 store data and 2010 tracts. Because LRAM uses 2019 store data, some tracts classified as hidden food deserts may have gained a large grocery store by 2025, so the number of hidden tracts may be overestimated; the next LRAM update will allow a same-year comparison.

PLACES estimates are model-based rather than directly measured; because they incorporate age, race/ethnicity, sex, education and poverty, associations with neighborhood characteristics partly reflect demographic composition, sub-county validation is limited, and CDC cautions against using them to evaluate interventions (Greenlund et al., 2022). PLACES estimates cover adults aged 18 years and older only; diabetes and prediabetes among youth are not captured here and require school-and clinic-based data sources, which I address in planned follow-up work. Because PLACES estimates are modeled from demographic composition, they are smoothed toward predicted values and may understate the most extreme tracts; my counts of doubleburden tracts and the adults living in them may therefore be conservative. To reduce bias from shared data sources, food-access and socioeconomic measures were taken from USDA and the Census Bureau rather than from PLACES itself (Yahaya et al., 2026; Tanner et al., 2024).

Results can change depending on the size of the areas studied (Bhagavathula & Williams, 2026). I measured diabetes and food access for the same census tracts, but the results still describe neighborhoods, not individual people.

My measures also assume that people buy food near home. That is not always true: GPS data from the Hartford, Connecticut, area showed that most restaurant customers came from outside the census tract where the restaurant was located (Jin et al., 2023). This problem is likely smaller for households without a car, because they cannot easily travel farther.

Finally, USDA measures count stores, not whether those stores sell foods that fit people's culture. In San Diego, having more Asian American and Pacific Islander restaurants nearby was linked to lower diabetes in that community, while the USDA supermarket measure was not consistently linked (Xie et al., 2025). This may matter in diverse areas such as Los Angeles and Metro Detroit.

Generalizability: California and Michigan differ in climate, transit, store mix, Medicaid food-is-medicine policy and population composition, and prior tract-level studies in Southern California and New York City identified different leading correlates of diabetes (Descarpentrie et al., 2025; Tanner et al., 2024). Comparing whole states, urban and rural tracts separately, and officially defined metropolitan areas reduces the risk that differences reflect how regions were drawn. Findings should still be read as specific to these two states, although the method uses only national public datasets and can be repeated in any US region.

5. Conclusion

Diabetes and poor food access overlap in fewer places than expected, but the newest USDA map hides many of them, especially in Metro Detroit. In this pilot, three AI chatbots gave healthy diabetes advice, yet they did not check whether patients could buy that food near home. Before AI tells patients what to eat, it needs to know where they live. A simple place-aware check, built from free public data, could make that possible.

3.5

Pilot audit of AI meal advice I scored all 60 chatbot answers (20 from each chatbot). The advice was healthy in almost every answer. All 60 included non-starchy vegetables, whole grains or beans, and lean protein. Every answer mentioned cost and getting to a store without a car. I found no unsafe advice. The chatbots differed on two points. ChatGPT (20 of 20) and Claude (18 of 20) said what to drink, but Gemini did so in only 1 of 20 answers. Advice to limit added sugar or refined carbohydrates appeared in 16 ChatGPT, 20 Claude and 17 Gemini answers.
